title: You Can Add Thousands of Online Friends, Yet Your Brain Caps Real Ties Near One Fifty

acts.name: 1992 UCL 38-Primate Neocortex Ratio Test Against the Fruit-Map Myth
sentences: You think social apps gave humans limitless real friends!
Yet ancient biology still caps every circle tightly!
doctors first saw this in Robin Dunbar's Social Brain Discovery.
Total nightmare with the fruit myth.
Scientists thought primates grew big brains to find fruit.
In nineteen ninety-two, Robin Dunbar tested thirty-eight primate groups.
Brains burn twenty percent of fuel, like a bright spotlight.
Dunbar compared cortex size against territory and troop size.
Territory failed completely — and that wasn't the strangest part.

acts.name: 4.1 Human Neocortex Ratio & The 150 Social-Group Prediction
sentences: Why did troop size match brain size so tightly?
Larger troops always carried a bigger outer thinking layer.
The prefrontal cortex, your planner, grew as alliances expanded.
Humans hit a four point one ratio, like a four-story tower.
That primate line predicted one hundred forty-eight human ties.
Dunbar rounded that cap to one hundred fifty, like a village hall.
Fruit maps scattered wildly, while troop size aligned cleanly.
Farming clans split at one hundred fifty, like a full lifeboat.
Managing larger crowds without rules was a total nightmare.

acts.name: Combinatorial Alliance Tracking Across Prefrontal & Temporal Cortex
sentences: Why does direct peer trust break past that threshold?
Every newcomer multiplies social pairs across the whole group.
Instead of mapping trees, your brain tracks shifting favors.
Your prefrontal cortex, your planner, weighs who trusts whom.
Meanwhile, the temporal lobe, the side of the brain, stores identities.
Army units clustered near one hundred fifty, like a ferry boat.
You recognize one thousand five hundred faces, like a concert crowd.
Knowing faces takes far less fuel than keeping trust.
But here's the twist: how many allies hold you in crisis?

acts.name: Concentric 5 / 15 / 50 / 150 Circles & The 2011 Online Network Test
sentences: Inside your outer ring sit tighter circles of closeness.
Five close allies take forty percent of time, like five pillars.
Next sit fifteen friends and fifty peers, like nested bowls.
Did social media finally smash that primate ceiling?
In twenty eleven, scientists audited huge online networks.
Users gathered one thousand contacts, like a crowded plaza.
Mutual replies flattened near one hundred fifty, like a narrow bridge.
So did fast servers upgrade your social brain?

acts.name: 2021 Confidence Bands, 24-Hour Time Clocks & Human-Sized Teams
sentences: Servers upgraded storage, never human relationship bandwidth.
In twenty twenty-one, Patrik Lindenfors noted wider bands.
Personal circles span one hundred to two hundred fifty, like a sliding gauge.
Written laws let millions cooperate across modern cities.
Still, twenty-four daily hours lock care, like an hourglass.
Agile workplaces split teams near one hundred fifty, like modular cabins.
The data shocked the entire lab
Primate brain math still governs human trust.

acts.name: Protecting Your Inner Five Circle in an Age of Shallow Feeds
sentences: How should you spend social time this week?
Stop mistaking passive likes for a real safety net.
Your prefrontal cortex, your planner, needs unhurried talk for trust.
Your temporal lobe, the side of the brain, deepens bonds in person.
Guard two weekly hours for five allies, like five warm lamps.
Put phones away so friends get your full mind.
Depth beats headcount in every stage of life.
In everyday life, that means servers scale broadcasts, yet biology guards real closeness.
